The values of this functor satisfy the domain conditions wherever their operations are defined, and we characterize when the operations are defined exactly where these conditions hold. The functor induced by a composite receives a natural inclusion from the composite of the induced functors; this inclusion, which can be strict, makes the induced functors a normal lax indexed category. In finite dimensions, generalized hep-derivors realize graduation and unification as an equivalence between the homogeneous and heterogeneous presentations, and discretization as a left adjoint to truncation. In dimension $ω$, we reconstruct the categories of $ω$-categorial algebras as projective limits of their finite-dimensional truncations and obtain unification by a quotient construction; we also establish algebraic squares and compatibility with change of signature. Finally, for nonempty sets of sorts, we show that the finite-dimension condition in the homogeneous $ω$-presentation is not axiomatizable by quasi-existence equations on its fixed signature.
papers.lean_note: All definitions and results are formalized in Lean 4 on Mathlib, produced by AI agents, with a public repository and no unproved statements.

papers.title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
papers.abstract: Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.
papers.lean_note: AI agents generate Lean 4 proofs of toric-code Hamiltonian properties and spectral-gap perturbation bounds certifying that a superconducting device Hamiltonian retains the code space.

papers.title: ScienceCUA: Resource-to-Skill Construction and Execution-Guided Skill Evolution for Scientific Computer Use Agents
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.
papers.lean_note: Lean 4 (v4.14.0) is one of six scientific applications. Agents solve formal-proof tasks in it, and the authors audited and added Lean benchmark tasks.

papers.title: Asymptotically Optimal Weighted Edge Colorings via Local Bin Packing
papers.abstract: We study weighted edge coloring, where each edge of a graph $G$ has a weight in $(0,1]$, and colors are assigned so that the incident weight of each color at every vertex is at most one. The objective is to minimize the number of colors, denoted by $χ'_w(G)$. This generalizes classical edge coloring (all weights are one) and bin packing ($G$ is a star). Two natural lower bounds are the maximum weighted degree $Δ_w(G)$ and the maximum local bin-packing number $\mathrm{bp}(G)$: the maximum, over vertices, of the minimum number of unit bins needed to pack the incident weights. We have $\lceilΔ_w(G)\rceil\le\mathrm{bp}(G)\leχ'_w(G)$. How closely these local lower bounds approximate the global optimum is a longstanding open problem. Our main result establishes an asymptotic weighted analogue of Vizing's theorem: every simple graph admits a coloring using at most $(1+o(1))\mathrm{bp}(G)$ colors. Thus local bin packings can be made globally consistent with asymptotically vanishing relative loss, even in nonbipartite graphs. Our local-to-global rounding framework coordinates feasible local packing distributions into a partial coloring, leaving only $o(\mathrm{bp}(G))$ uncolored weight at every vertex. For bipartite multigraphs, we prove $χ'_w(G)\le(2+o(1))Δ_w(G)$, establishing the Chung--Ross conjecture [SICOMP'91] asymptotically. For loopless multigraphs, we obtain the exact bound $χ'_w(G)\le3\lceilΔ_w(G)\rceil$. Both leading coefficients are optimal, giving weighted analogues of the classical Kőnig--Shannon bounds. Further upper and lower bounds show that the classical factor-$3/2$ separation does not persist with the local bin-packing benchmark. We also disprove the exact weighted-degree conjecture of Feige and Singh [ESA'08]. Our upper bounds have polynomial-time algorithms, and their existence statements are formalized in Lean 4.
papers.lean_note: The five upper-bound existence statements for weighted edge coloring are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, AI-assisted, in a companion repository.

papers.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
papers.abstract: We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$--$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries. For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.
papers.lean_note: Develops a Lean 4 library for cut-query algorithms that formalizes the paper's certificate and deterministic minimum-cut results, with an appendix mapping theorems to Lean statements.

papers.title: What makes a theorem interesting? Operationalizing interestingness for open-ended exploration
papers.abstract: An agent that explores, whether it generates conjectures or research ideas, must decide which of them are worth keeping. This judgment of interestingness is usually delegated to a hand-picked proxy or to a language model, neither of which is known to correspond to what humans actually value. I study it for mathematical theorems, by observing which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and in papers. I model each way of singling out results as an evaluator that weights features of a result's statement, its proof and dependencies, and split its weights into a shared and a subjective part. In formalized mathematics, ex-ante features predict these selections as well as a large language-model judge, and the two complement each other. Interestingness is also largely shared. One set of weights, carried mostly by structural features such as the length of the statement and of the proof and the subfields the proof draws on, accounts for most of the signal and transfers in part across formal libraries. What remains subjective depends on practices and individual authors more than on subfields. The judge's advantage lies in its knowledge of the canon, and neither the judge nor the features rely on memory of the papers. The approach, which infers what a community finds interesting from what it singles out, can be applied to other sciences.
papers.lean_note: Uses Mathlib's hand-written theorems, with statement, proof and dependency features and curated 'main results' labels, as the main corpus for modeling theorem interestingness.

papers.title: Reap: Uncovering Monte Carlo proof search with a lightweight model
papers.abstract: We present Reap, an open framework for learning and analyzing formal proof search in Lean4. Reap implements policy-value-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search directly in Lean, sharing proof-state transitions, AND-OR search, and replay verification between inference and training rollouts. Structured action logs expose how neural predictions and tactic execution interact during search. Using this framework, we train Reaper-1, a 1.7B-parameter policy-value model, through continued pre-training, supervised tactic learning, and iterative search-based reinforcement learning. Using a separate premise selector, the final system solves 79.9% of miniF2F-test at pass@32, establishing state-of-the-art performance among open provers of comparable size while remaining competitive with substantially larger models. Beyond improved solve rates, our results suggest that RL strengthens the prover's ability to organize proofs around useful intermediate results, favoring substantial advances over repeated local adjustments. This more directed proof construction is accompanied by increasingly elaborate tactic programs: fewer explicit search decisions are needed, while more work is performed within each decision. The resulting trade-off between search effort and tactic execution cost provides insight into how learning changes the prover's problem-solving strategy.
papers.lean_note: Implements policy-value-guided MCTS proof search as a Lean 4 tactic via Lean metaprogramming, then trains and evaluates a 1.7B prover on Lean benchmarks.

papers.title: On Lattice Tilings by Symmetric Limited Magnitude Error Balls: Q-polynomials and Ideal Characterization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the lattice tilings of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by the symmetric limited magnitude error balls $\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)$, which play a crucial role in flash memory applications. Using generating functions and complete Bell polynomials, we derive an explicit formula for the $r$-th Q-polynomial associated with $\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)$. Then, an ideal-theoretic characterization of the lattice tiling condition is developed: for an odd prime $p$ dividing $|\mathcal{B}(n,t,k,k)|$ exactly once, a lattice tiling would force a certain polynomial to lie outside a certain ideal of $\mathbb{F}_p[Y_1,\dots,Y_{\frac{p-1}{2}}]$. Applying this criterion yields congruence conditions on the dimension $n$ that rule out lattice tilings; for $2\le t\le10$ and $1\le k\le10$, a systematic Maple computation over all primes $3\le p\le29$ excludes, on average, $35.65\%$ of all dimensions, with a maximum of $76.69\%$. Finally, we obtain two infinite families of parameters $(n,t,k)$ for which no lattice tiling exists: no lattice tiling exists if $k\equiv4\pmod9$ and the base-$3$ addition of $t$ and $n-1-t$ produces exactly one carry; and no lattice tiling of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by $\mathcal{B}(n,n-1,k,k)$ exists if $k\equiv8\pmod9$ and $n\equiv2,4\pmod6$. Their sizes are also estimated.
papers.lean_note: All statements except those relying on Maple computations are formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using only standard axioms.

papers.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.
papers.lean_note: Implements a Lean 4 runtime that checks agent tool calls against Lean policies, proves the decision procedure equivalent to LeanLTL semantics, and uses metaprogramming for proof-guided repair.

papers.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
papers.abstract: A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight. A law of softmax attention predicts that a growing crowd of bounded scores dilutes the attention on any patch or register whose score stays fixed. The same law gives a remedy that needs no training: multiply every score, the sink's included, by the ratio of the logarithms of the test and training token counts. Given sufficient margins at the training resolution, this keeps the attention on a match when one is present, and on a sink such as a register when none is, though trained models need not meet those margins. We test these predictions in public vision transformers and in controlled models read far above their training token count. Attention spreads as predicted. Registers lose their share, though production models compensate in part, and the rescaling holds the share of DINOv2's registers nearly level. Applied at test time without training, the rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy in nearly every model, with absolute or rotary positions and with registers, and on images with native detail. The calibrated multiplier rises with the logarithmic ratio on average and varies across models. Its rise is steeper than the square-root rule used in image generators; in controlled models the log ratio is also more accurate, while in the public models the two rules' accuracy difference remains unresolved. The rescaling does not restore the attention a model learned, and why it helps, beyond countering the dilution, remains open.
papers.lean_note: Every mathematical statement about softmax attention dilution and the log-ratio rescaling is proved in Lean 4 and released as ancillary files.

papers.title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
papers.abstract: When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering. First, we establish a logic-agnostic foundation combining a spec-first stack inversion, a zero-code-review workflow gated by automated continuous integration (CI) checks, and a minimal Verification Intermediate Representation (VIR) lowered via a thin, verified translator. Second, we pair an extensional Computational Type Theory (CTT) specification layer with Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS) and linear resource typing in the VIR--eliminating rewrite friction for synthesis agents while defining an experiment, its protocol frozen before the first reader, to measure whether removing boundary coercions improves human specification readability. Third, we scale collaboration across multi-team organizations using Personal Spec-Copilots and a Shared Synthesis Fleet that detects cross-team Semantic Merge Conflicts and fuses modular contracts into zero-copy binaries. We illustrate this architecture on a zero-copy authenticated message router and distinguish our existing empirical baselines (salt, SaltBench, x86lean, and MetaPRL) from newly proposed components.
papers.lean_note: Builds on the authors' Lean 4 artifacts (salt review gates, x86lean ISA semantics, vir IR) and contrasts idiomatic Lean specifications with extensional CTT.

papers.title: Exact Shortest Paths and Maximum Flow in Planar Networks in the CONGEST Model
papers.abstract: In the CONGEST model, exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) with nonnegative weights and exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks have both been solved in $\tilde O(D^2)$ rounds, where $D$ is the hop diameter, while the lower bound is $Ω(D)$. Given the approximate distance labels of a recent preprint (arXiv:2606.31192), which we use as a black box, we solve exact directed SSSP in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. It rests on a lemma that answers queries from a virtual source with the labels, and on a corrected discretization of the reduction of exact to approximate distances (arXiv:2210.16351). All further bounds of the form $\tilde O(D)$ and $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ use these labels. Through the reduction of arXiv:2303.00811, SSSP with negative weights, or the detection of a negative cycle, takes $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ rounds with high probability. We weight the face-disjoint graph of arXiv:2411.11718 so that its distances are dual distances, which turns distance problems in the dual into problems in a planar network of hop diameter $O(D)$. This gives exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks in $\min\{\tilde O(D^2),D\cdot n^{o(1)}\}$ rounds with high probability, and in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds with $s,t$ on a common face. In undirected planar networks, the value of a minimum $st$-cut and a minimum cut take $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. For this we repair the auxiliary graphs of arXiv:2608.09500 at $s$ and $t$, and we show that its recursion, as we read it, can miss the minimum cut, also with exact shortest paths: on a network with $11$ vertices it reports $37$ for a minimum cut of $15$. Two more shortest-path computations per level make it exact. The virtual-source lemma, the weighting of the face-disjoint graph and the corrected discretization are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; all other arguments are proved on paper only. Numerical checks are not used in any proof.
papers.lean_note: Three key lemmas (virtual-source lemma, dual distance lemma for the face-disjoint graph, discretized boosting step) are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, sorry-free.

papers.title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
papers.abstract: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. Calibration measures (Brier score, log-loss) and ranking measures (nDCG, AUC) fall outside it. We close the gap with two further classes of cell operators: deviation operators phi(y - yhat), which give a Calibration Framework, and rank- and slice-dependent operators (positional gains for DCG, column concordance cells for AUC), which give a Ranking Framework. Both inherit the micro/macro/exemplar aggregation architecture. For calibration, the three Brier aggregations collapse to one scalar; the Murphy decomposition holds in matrix form (unbinned, binned and isotonic); and, within the Brier-type class-indexed family, a measure is skew-invariant if and only if it depends only on the class-conditional errors alpha_j and beta_j, the calibration analogues of recall and specificity. For ranking, raw DCG collapses across aggregations while nDCG does not; per-class nDCG and per-class AUC are related by a row-column duality; micro-AUC differs from pooled ROC-AUC; raw positional scores are never strictly proper, and nDCG and AUC need not be proper. The skew-invariant per-class building blocks share one class-conditional expectation template. Experiments on two multilabel benchmarks illustrate the distinctions. Many of the results are machine-checked in Lean 4; the proofs, the experiments and the aggmetrics.scores package are public: https://github.com/rcprati/discrimination-calibration-ranking
papers.lean_note: Many calibration and ranking results, including skew-invariance characterizations and Brier collapse, are machine-checked in Lean 4 against Mathlib; the proofs are in a public repository.

papers.title: A proof of the sharpness conjectures for all saturated fusion systems
papers.abstract: We prove the Díaz$\unicode[Arial]{x2013}$Park conjecture for sharpness of saturated fusion systems. More generally, for every saturated fusion system $\mathcal F$ over a finite $p$-group and every Mackey functor for $\mathcal F$ over the localisation $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of the integers at $p$, the higher limits of its contravariant part over the centric orbit category vanish in all positive degrees. In particular, the subgroup and normaliser decompositions of every $p$-local finite group $(S,\mathcal F,\mathcal L)$ over the $\mathcal F$-centric subgroups are sharp. This answers in the affirmative a question in the list of important open problems in [M. Aschbacher, R. Kessar and B. Oliver, Fusion Systems in Algebra and Topology, Cambridge Univ. Press (2011)], and proves the sharpness conjecture stated in [M. Aschbacher and B. Oliver, Fusion systems, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (2016)] and Conjecture 1.2 of [E. Yalç$\unicode[Arial]{x131}$n, Higher limits over the fusion orbit category, Adv. Math. (2022)]. The proof is algebraic and does not rely on the classification of finite simple groups.
papers.lean_note: Main theorem and corollary formalised unconditionally in Lean (about 62k lines, Codex-assisted) and Rocq, checked with Nanoda and comparator; repository provided.

papers.title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
papers.abstract: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time, instead of checking every single line of generated code. LARK formalizes the GPU machine model and the semantics of each operation in Lean 4 once per target language, and the Lean 4 semantics of any incoming kernel is derived from these pre-built definitions. LLM agents then automate the proof in two steps. First, an agent decomposes the whole kernel semantics into smaller segments and Lean 4 verifies this segmentation, which addresses the intractability of proving equivalence for large kernels directly. Second, agents write Lean proofs that each kernel segment matches its high-level PyTorch counterpart. Together, the two steps give whole-program equivalence. We demonstrate that LARK can be used 1) to ensure correctness in existing code-generation agents and 2) to automatically verify human-written kernel libraries. On the KernelCraft GPU tasks, combined with a simple ReAct agent, LARK enables GLM 5.3 to fully verify 10 of 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all 5 Level-2 kernels. Moreover, over 10 production kernels randomly sampled from popular open-source LLM serving frameworks, LARK verifies 9 and identifies a new data race bug in the tenth. We believe LARK represents a significant step toward verifiable code generation in the agentic era.
papers.lean_note: Formalizes a GPU machine model and PTX/CUDA/HIP operation semantics in Lean 4; LLM agents write Lean proofs of kernel equivalence to PyTorch specifications.

papers.title: Monotone Local Search with Sample-Dependent Running Times
papers.abstract: Monotone Local Search turns an algorithm that extends a given partial solution into an algorithm that finds a solution from scratch: sample a few elements, hope that they lie in an unknown solution, and complete them. Its known analyses bound every call of the extension algorithm by a worst-case time that depends only on the number of sampled elements, and Esmer et al. (SODA 2024) showed that no algorithm that uses the extension algorithm as a black box with this running time beats the original form by more than a polynomial factor. We let this running time depend on the actual sample. If the extension algorithm decides in time $O^*(2^{g(I,X,k)})$, for a polynomial-time computable $g$, whether a sample $X$ can be completed to a solution with at most $k$ elements, our main theorem gives a randomized algorithm with one-sided error in time $O^*(2^{ψn})$ whenever, for some solution $S$ of size $k$ and some $t$, the exponential moment $\sum_{X\subseteq S,|X|=t}2^{-g(I,X,k)}$ is at least $2^{-ψn}\binom{n}{t}$. A corollary, multivariate Monotone Local Search, generalizes the theorems of Fomin et al. (STOC 2016, J. ACM 2019) and of Gaspers and Lee (ICALP 2017). For Max Leaf Spanning Tree and, equivalently, Connected Dominating Set, the previous best polynomial-space bound is $O^*(1.8619^n)$. Completing a sample is a Steiner tree problem, solved in time exponential in the number of terminals, which varies strongly with the sample. We obtain a randomized polynomial-space algorithm in time $O(1.6991^n)$ and a deterministic one in time $(\sqrt5-\frac12)^n 2^{o(n)}=O(1.7361^n)$. For connectivity problems in which the extension algorithm's running time doubles with every component of the sample, an analysis through a partition function gives randomized polynomial-space algorithms in time $O^*(1.8^n)$ for Connected Feedback Vertex Set and $O(1.6444^n)$ for Connected Vertex Cover.
papers.lean_note: Parts of the running-time analysis, including the certificates and the correctness of the Steiner extension, are formally checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib in the ancillary files.

papers.title: Computation in Anonymous Directed Dynamic Networks: Exact Worst-Case Termination Time and Network-Wise Intractability
papers.abstract: We determine the exact round complexity of Counting in anonymous directed dynamic networks. Agents have no identifiers, but $\ell\geq1$ of them are designated as leaders. Every agent knows $\ell$ and its own leader status, while the population size $n$ is unknown and has to be determined by the agents. Communication proceeds in synchronous rounds; the directed communication graph may change arbitrarily and unpredictably from one round to the next, but is assumed to remain strongly connected. We solve Counting with a distributed algorithm that makes every agent output $n$ and halt after a number of rounds equal to $\begin{cases} n&\text{if }n=\ell\\ 2n-1&\text{if }n>\ell\text{ and }\ell=1\\ 2n-2&\text{if }n>\ell\text{ and }\ell\geq2. \end{cases}$ The algorithm works even for networks with loops and parallel arcs and even when agents learn their outdegree only after sending. We prove that this bound is worst-case tight over directed multigraphs for every $n$ and $\ell$ with $1\leq\ell\leq n$. Moreover, the local computation is polynomial (provided that each communication multigraph has at most $2^{\operatorname{poly}(n)}$ arcs): in every round, each agent solves at most one linear system with up to $n$ variables. By standard techniques, solving Counting also enables the evaluation of any computable function of the multiset of agents' input values within $2n-1$ communication rounds. The bound above optimizes the worst case over all networks. For an individual network, we show that even deciding whether an agent already has enough local information to determine $n$ is $\mathsf{coNP}$-complete (provided that the numbers of parallel arcs are encoded in binary). Thus, worst-case-optimal Counting admits polynomial local computation, whereas exact network-wise optimization is intractable under standard complexity assumptions.
papers.lean_note: All results, including the termination bounds and coNP-completeness, are formally proved in Lean, with AI assistance, in a public repository.

papers.title: VeriBase: Automated Construction of Theorem Libraries for Software Verification
papers.abstract: Software verification is typically more challenging than coding. Software developers routinely build on mature libraries and APIs, but turning successful verification solutions into reusable libraries still requires substantial expert effort. In this paper, we propose VeriBase, a framework for automatically constructing software-verification libraries by jointly generalizing code and its associated theorems from successful verification solutions. The key challenge is to generalize implementations together with the theorem statements and proofs that depend on these implementations, and reconcile overlapping components across verification tasks. To this end, VeriBase treats code and its associated theorems as declaration families, and designs a three-phase pipeline, which proves seed tasks, generalizes code and associated theorems, and harvests the resulting families into shared interfaces. VeriBase updates dependent declarations as interface change and uses Lean to check the resulting code and proofs. We evaluate VeriBase across four benchmarks with three backend LLMs. The results show that the general-purpose library built from independent 4,191 programs increases the average task success rate by up to 17.0% and meanwhile reduces the proof completion time by up to 21.4%. When VeriBase constructs a benchmark-specific library, further improvement can be observed.
papers.lean_note: Builds Lean 4 software-verification libraries from LLM-generated, Lean-checked solutions, and evaluates them on Lean benchmarks (Verina, FVAPPS, VeriContest, VeriSoftBench).

papers.title: A new upper bound for the irrationality exponent of $ζ(5)$
papers.abstract: Fauzan's determinantal proof that $ζ(5)$ is irrational also yields $|ζ(5)-a/b|>b^{-260}$ for all large $b$. The exponent is the product $\varrhoλ/\varepsilon$ of three constants attached to the construction, of which $\varrho$ governs the growth of a relative matrix norm. We show that $\varrho$ may be taken to be $9.09$ instead of $6933/500=13.866$, and deduce $|ζ(5)-a/b|>b^{-171}$ for all integers $a$ and all sufficiently large integers $b$, so that the irrationality exponent of $ζ(5)$ is at most $171$. Two closed-form functions replace two worst-case estimates: a node function, which bounds the residue weights individually instead of uniformly, and the external field of the energy estimate, which replaces a factor-by-factor bound on the weight. The result is conditional on Fauzan's preprint. An exact arithmetic verifier is attached.
papers.lean_note: Relies on a credited third-party Lean 4/Mathlib formalization of Fauzan's ζ(5) irrationality proof, so its hypotheses are machine-checked modulo the prime number theorem.

papers.title: A log-concavity criterion for finite nonnegative linearization
papers.abstract: In a 2005 survey, R. Szwarc asked for criteria, stated in the recurrence coefficients, for nonnegative linearization (property (P)) of finite orthogonal polynomial systems such as the Krawtchouk polynomials. For a finite three-term recurrence normalized to have row sums one, whose diagonal and downward coefficients have a constant nonnegative ratio, we prove that property (P) holds for every product, including products beyond the terminal degree, whenever the Newton coefficients of the profile $d_i=b_i+c_i$ are log-concave without internal zeros. The criterion contains the full positive Krawtchouk range and the dual $q$-Krawtchouk arrays, and through a quadratic decomposition of symmetric finite systems it covers Szwarc's quadratic system $Q_n$ in its sharp range $0<p_0\leq1/2$. As a limit to any such criterion, property (P) fails at coefficient distance $O((1-r^2)^N)$ from the Krawtchouk array of size $N$ with fixed ratio $c_i/d_i=r<1$. All theorems, corollaries and propositions are formalized in Lean 4.
papers.lean_note: All theorems, corollaries, propositions and key lemmas are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib in companion code, and exact counterexample computations are machine-verified.

papers.title: Deterministic $n^{O(\log n)}$ Graph Isomorphism Algorithm via Inherited Decompositions
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic $n^{O(\log d)}$-time algorithm for isomorphism of graphs with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $d$. Since $d<n$, this is an $n^{O(\log n)}$-time algorithm for graph isomorphism. To our knowledge, this is the first proof of such a worst-case bound for general graphs. It improves the explicit cubic logarithmic exponent in the analysis of the corrected Luks--Babai algorithm. For graphs of maximum degree $d$, the best previous bound known to us, due to Grohe, Neuen, and Schweitzer, is $n^{O((\log d)^c)}$ for an absolute constant $c$. The algorithm uses the local-certificate and color-refinement steps of Babai's quasipolynomial algorithm, but retains the decomposition of each recursive instance when it solves an auxiliary coloring problem. There are two reasons for retaining this information. First, a local test can make progress without removing many vertices: it can eliminate a layer of permutation symmetry. A logarithmic bound on the total weight of these layers allows tests of constant size. Second, the auxiliary bipartite graphs arising in the symmetry-breaking step can be represented inside the current instance, after retaining a row decomposition when necessary. These recursive calls inherit the progress already made. Two further observations give the dependence on the degree. The recursive calls made by a local test check disjoint parts of the instance, so together they cost about as much as one call on the whole instance. And for graphs of maximum degree $d$, each large symmetric action that the algorithm must break acts on at most $d$ points. We present the algorithm through colorings, partitions, and bipartite graphs, and collect the permutation-group ingredients in one appendix. The result extends to string isomorphism and returns one isomorphism and generators for the full automorphism group.
papers.lean_note: Lean files formalizing the main theorem, a deterministic n^{O(log n)} graph isomorphism bound, are provided on GitHub.

papers.title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
papers.abstract: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.
papers.lean_note: Builds a Lean 4 tool that fingerprints elaborated statements, runs kernel-checked challenges on them, and gates patches; it is evaluated on Mathlib revisions and LLM agents.

papers.title: Truly Every Author is First Author: Equal-Width Superimposition by Minimising Visual Distortion
papers.abstract: In an earlier work, Demaine and Demaine propose that every author be a first author by superimposing all author names on the same spot of the title page. The construction is typographically unstable, because names have different natural widths. The superimposed block is ragged and the longest name dominates the visual mass, reintroducing exactly the ordering advantage the standard removes. We close this loophole. Each name is distorted by two knobs, a horizontal glyph scale and an inter-letter tracking, until all names occupy one common width $W$. We give a quadratic distortion model, solve the per-name trade-off in closed form by Lagrange multipliers, and show that the total-distortion optimal common width is a stiffness-weighted mean of the natural widths. We provide implementations as a $\LaTeX$ package and a Typst package, covering author blocks and bibliography entries alike; this paper typesets its own author block and its own reference with the former. Every proposition is machine-checked in Lean. The $\LaTeX$ and Typst packages, as well as the proofs, are available at https://github.com/MrP01/EveryAuthorIsFirstAuthor.
papers.lean_note: Every proposition of the distortion model, including the per-name optimal split and the optimal common width, is machine-checked in Lean, with proofs released on GitHub.

papers.title: A Numerical Refinement of an Exact Discrete Fourier Transform Bound
papers.abstract: We refine the numerical bounds in Kartal's instantiation of Sussman's exact discrete Fourier transform construction. For every integer n >= 1, the resulting algorithm computes the length-n transform with work O(n (log n)^(1 - delta)), where delta = 0.0030201659. The bound holds in an exact complex-arithmetic RAM model with a supplied canonical root of unity. This final exponent saving exceeds the earlier certified parameter C_0 = 0.00302016 by 5.9 x 10^(-9). We retain the underlying circuit, tighten rational bounds for sums of powers of its block and target ranks, and increase the fixed tensor power from 7760 to 11640. These bounds establish the inequalities for Sussman's recursion at the intermediate certificate parameter C = 0.00302016595. The gap C - delta absorbs the overhead of recursion and Fourier reduction. The resulting transform theorem is proved in Lean and checked against the reference problem statement.
papers.lean_note: The DFT work-bound theorem and convolution corollary are proved in Lean 4 and checked against a reference specification using Comparator. The Lean development is released as an artifact.

papers.title: Uniform cubic bounds for irrational values of the dilogarithm
papers.abstract: We study explicit denominator conditions ensuring the irrationality of the dilogarithm at positive and negative rational points. We prove that $\operatorname{Li}_2(p/q)$ is irrational whenever $q>(4e^4/27)p^3$, and obtain an explicit, slightly smaller threshold for $\operatorname{Li}_2(-p/q)$. The positive argument specializes the Rhin--Viola integral family and uses a uniform estimate for a restricted prime divisor. The negative argument combines the same arithmetic construction with three adjacent integral moments and an explicit maximization. We also give finite-numerator refinements by interpolating certified partition bounds and by introducing a comparison measure with a quadratic tail. In particular, $\operatorname{Li}_2(5/q)$ is irrational for every integer $q\ge418$. The proof separates the established integral and determinant constructions from the parameter estimates and finite certificates used here.
papers.lean_note: The new estimates and deductions for dilogarithm irrationality thresholds are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, building on a pinned Lean development (Li2Rational).

papers.title: Maximal input entropy for binary two-deletion and two-insertion channels
papers.abstract: Under uniform transmission, we determine the received binary words that maximize input entropy for two-deletion and two-insertion channels. For two deletions the maximizers are exactly the two alternating words at every positive received length. For two insertions the same conclusion holds from received length five onward; we give all smaller cases and exact maximal values. The proof combines an embedding-count identity organized by runs with strict convexity estimates, and a grouping of two-position deletion masks. For every insertion radius we give the complete positive embedding histogram of an alternating received word. We also determine its three-deletion histogram for every length, and certify all three-deletion maximizers through received length twelve and all three-insertion maximizers through length eighteen by exact integer comparison. These computations give precise three-error conjectures with their small-length exceptions.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem's maximizer characterizations and maximal entropy formulas for two-deletion/two-insertion channels are formalized in a Lean companion supplied as ancillary files.

papers.title: The Golden Quadruple: Four Reals Whose Differences Form a Geometric Progression, Rigidity of the Golden Ratio, and a Bohr Almost Periodic Cosine Sum
papers.abstract: Let $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. The set $\{0,\varphi,\varphi^2,\varphi^3\}$ is classical (Euclid, Elements XIII.8): by $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ its six pairwise differences take the values $1,\varphi,\varphi^2,\varphi^3$, with multiplicities $1,2,2,1$. We write it as the golden quadruple $S=(F, F-a, F-b, F-a-b)$, $a=\varphi u$, $b=\varphi^2u$, $F>a+b$, and study its extremal and rigidity properties. No five distinct reals have all their positive differences in $\{u\varphi^n:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$; this follows from a result of Lenstra (1977), and we give a self-contained proof. We give an elementary proof of uniqueness: every four-element set with this property is a translate of $u\varphi^m\{0,\varphi,\varphi^2,\varphi^3\}$ for some $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, and if all its differences lie in $\{u,\varphi u,\varphi^2u,\varphi^3u\}$ it is a translate of $S$. Among all $x>1$, only $x=\varphi$ admits a four-point set of reals whose set of distinct differences is $\{c,cx,cx^2,cx^3\}$. For the analogous quadruple with base $x\neq\varphi$ the failure is measured by two closure residues, which along Fibonacci quotients equal $\pm u/\mathrm{Fib}_n^2$ and $\pm \mathrm{Fib}_{n+1}u/\mathrm{Fib}_n^3$. The cosine sum $C_S(t)=\sum\cos(2πd t)$ over the six differences equals $8\cos^2(πa t)\cos^2(πb t)-2$; it is not periodic but is Bohr almost periodic, with explicit almost periods $τ_n=\mathrm{Fib}_n/u$, and we determine the two-term asymptotics $\sup_t|C_S(t+τ_n)-C_S(t)|=6\sqrt3 π\varphi^{-n}-2\sqrt3 π^3\varphi^{-3n}+O(\varphi^{-5n})$, with optimal constants; the inclusion length of the $\varepsilon$-almost periods is of order $1/\varepsilon$. For a scale $K>0$ the golden ladder $ν_n=K\varphi^{-n}$ realises the construction with differences $ν_{200},\dots,ν_{203}$; we evaluate it for $K=\sqrt{c^5/(Gh)}$. All proofs are elementary and self-contained.
papers.lean_note: The combinatorial and algebraic core results (difference multiset, uniqueness, base rigidity, cosine-sum closed form) are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, and the axioms are audited.

papers.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models
papers.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
papers.lean_note: The deterministic theoretical results about timestamp rules and valid-time memory are machine-checked in Lean 4 in a supplementary file, ReDate.lean.

papers.title: Promotion and Extension of General Escape-Covering Duality Relationship
papers.abstract: Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem, Moser's worm problem, Lebesgue's universal covering problems, and the classical 'fits and covers' questions can be organized by a common obstruction principle: an object fits a region if some admissible group action places it in the region, whereas an escape object is one for which every placement fails to remain in the interior. In this paper, we develop a general theory of escape-covering duality for any dimension and explore several applications. For convex translation covers of all closed planar curves of Euclidean length one, we prove $ W \ge f(\sqrt3/9)+c_1>0.15545785378555,c_1=0.000009944944227372... $ Here $f(\sqrt3/9)$ is Wetzel's classical lower bound. For a rational polytopal Minkowski gauge and prescribed rational facet directions, we express universal closed-loop cover feasibility as a rational polyhedron in the facet offsets. After removing translations, minimum volume is attained at a vertex. Refining the facet directions gives explicit two-sided rational bounds for the unrestricted fixed-gauge worm constant. Four exact benchmarks recover known sharp values. The construction uses an elementary circuit--circumradius form of the established non-fitting-polygon and capacity theory. We supply its support and ledger derivation, the finite complete test family in arbitrary dimension, a cover vertex bound, and the resulting algebraicity statement. The surrounding escape--covering framework includes endpoint placement, attainment, gauge stability, and finite-to-continuum error bounds. For nonsymmetric gauges the objects are parametrized closed curves, so orientation-dependent length is retained. Through the published capacity identity, the improved Wetzel estimate gives a product volume--capacity factor below $1.023781939711102$ for every planar ellipsoidal gauge.
papers.lean_note: Includes a Lean 4/Mathlib companion file stating a named theorem for each manuscript result, exposing the dependency graph; explicitly not an end-to-end formalization.

papers.title: A power-saving asymptotic for a Möbius-weighted GCD quadratic form
papers.abstract: For the Möbius-weighted quadratic form $T(N)=\sum_{m,n\leq N}μ(m)μ(n)(m,n)^2/(mn)$, we prove that $T(N)=cN+O_{\varepsilon}(N^{2/3+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, where $c>0$ is given by an absolutely convergent series of finite Möbius sums multiplied by a convergent Euler product. The proof combines the classical Jordan-totient decomposition of the GCD kernel with a mean-value estimate that is uniform in a coprimality parameter. Grouping the resulting squares according to $\lfloor N/d\rfloor$ gives the error term and a nonnegative series for $c$.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem's asymptotic, error estimate, convergence and positivity of the constant are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using no extra axioms.

papers.title: On the Distribution of Prime Squares and Its Applications
papers.abstract: We prove that, for every \(A>0\), all but \(O_A(X(\log X)^{-A})\) integers \(n<X\) satisfying \(n\equiv11\pmod{24}\) admit a representation \[ n=a^2+b^2+p^2, \] where \(p\) and \(a^2+b^2+1\) are prime and \((a,b)=1\). For ergodic averages along prime squares, we prove a universal divergence result for integrable functions, while establishing almost-everywhere convergence for near-integrable functions. We also quantify how the bounds used to establish convergence behave as one approaches integrability. Moreover, we prove endpoint improving and sparse bounds for the corresponding discrete averages, with an explicit Orlicz loss.
papers.lean_note: An accompanying Lean 4 formalization of the paper's results, generated with ChatGPT assistance, is publicly available but not yet independently reviewed.

papers.title: Order continuity of induced homomorphisms between free Banach lattices
papers.abstract: Let $T\colon F\to E$ be a bounded operator between Banach spaces and let $\overline T\colon FBL^{(p)}[F]\to FBL^{(p)}[E]$ be the lattice homomorphism induced by $T$ between the corresponding free $p$-convex Banach lattices generated by $F$ and $E$. We show that $\overline T$ is order continuous if and only if it is either zero or a lattice isomorphic embedding. For $p=\infty$, this holds precisely when $T$ is zero or an isomorphic embedding, while for $1\leq p<\infty$, apart from the zero operator, $T$ must be an embedding and the pair $(T(F),E)$ must have the operator-extension property POE-$p$. In addition, we study when $FBL^{(p)}[E]$ is order dense or majorizing in $FBL^{(q)}[E]$ for $p<q$.
papers.lean_note: All theorems, propositions, lemmas and corollaries are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib and the BanLat Banach lattice library, linked per statement.

papers.title: Blazing-Fast SMT-LIB Parsing for Rust and Lean
papers.abstract: SMT-LIB is a standard input format for Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers. However, parsing the format is non-trivial and can become a bottleneck, e.g. when retrieving benchmark metadata or normalising the input for solvers. We introduce blazing-smtlib, a Rust parsing library for SMT-LIB, and BSmtLib, its port to Lean. We outline the library API we designed for composability and extensibility (including non-standard SMT-LIB commands), and discuss our implementation decisions for fast lexing and parsing. We proved that our lexing and parsing with Lean-specific optimisations match our formalised reading of the SMT-LIB syntax. We measured performance on a representative sample from the 2025 SMT-LIB corpus and found that blazing-smtlib is more than 6 times faster on the geometric mean than previous parsing libraries and BSmtLib is faster or comparable to them.
papers.lean_note: Ports a Rust SMT-LIB parser to Lean (BSmtLib) and proves its optimised lexer and parser match a Lean formalisation of SMT-LIB syntax.

papers.title: Grassmann: The Coordinate-Independent Linear Algebra Programming Language
papers.abstract: Scientists, engineers, and mathematicians often formulate algorithms using coordinate-independent linear algebra because its tools are composable and harder to misuse. For numerical processing, however, users must translate these ideas into coordinate-dependent array code. Most practitioners do so prematurely because tools such as NumPy lack coordinate-independent representations, while existing languages with such constructs do not model enough linear algebra for the situations where they matter. We propose Grassmann, a small language bridging coordinate-independent linear algebra and coordinate-dependent implementations. It uses dependent types, linear types, and partially (pseudo-)invertible computation to model situations arising in exterior algebra and differential geometry. It targets the linear algebra at a point on a manifold, a prerequisite for many specifications in scientific computing and computer graphics. A language for coordinates lets users move between these representations. We give a denotational semantics assigning meaning without coordinates and an operational semantics translating Grassmann to array code under a choice of coordinates. Our main metatheoretic result shows that operational evaluations agree with the denotational semantics under an arbitrary choice of coordinates. This models how practitioners translate linear algebra for computers and suggests an approach to algorithmic optimization at a high level of abstraction. Our optimized implementation generates code for exterior algebra operations with overheads no more than 10%.
papers.lean_note: The language's metatheory (soundness of denotational semantics, adequacy of operational semantics, SVD/spectral results) is mechanized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: On Small Universal Reversible Turing Machines
papers.abstract: A reversible Turing machine (RTM) is a Turing machine in which every instantaneous description has at most one predecessor. Writing $\mathrm{URTM}(m,n)$ for a universal RTM with $m$ states and $n$ symbols, we construct $\mathrm{URTM}(3,600)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(4,38)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(5,36)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(6,28)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(7,26)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(8,21)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(9,8)$, $\mathrm{URTM}(10,7)$, and $\mathrm{URTM}(85,2)$; each of them has fewer states or fewer symbols than each of the nine URTMs in Morita's book (2017). Most of them come from improved versions of Morita's conversions to three states, to four states, and to two symbols; for example, the improved conversion to three states uses $O(mn^2)$ symbols instead of $O(m^2n^3)$. $\mathrm{URTM}(10,7)$ comes from merging two states of Morita's $\mathrm{URTM}(13,7)$, recording the difference in tags on the tape cells, and then merging symbols, three times; one more such step gives $\mathrm{URTM}(9,8)$. We also show that the halting problem of RTMs with at most two states is decidable for finite instantaneous descriptions, so that no RTM with at most two states is universal under any notion of universality that reduces the halting problem of Turing machines to it by a computable encoding into finite instantaneous descriptions; in particular, there is no URTM with at most two states in our formalization of Morita's definition. We also show that no three-state, two-symbol RTM is universal in that formalization.
papers.lean_note: All definitions and theorems, including the URTM constructions, universality proofs, and nonexistence results, are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with kernel-checked computations.

papers.title: Fluctuation bounds for rotationally invariant first-passage percolation
papers.abstract: We prove that in rotationally invariant first-passage percolation on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d\geq2$, the passage time $T_n$ over a distance $n$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\exp(|T_n-μn|/n^{\frac{1}{2}(1-\varepsilon)})]\leq C$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, where $μ$ is the time constant. This implies that its variance is at most a constant times $n^{1-\varepsilon}$, the bound that Basu, Sidoravicius and Sly proved in the planar case. As in their work, our argument is an induction on the scale, but in place of their proof that the geodesic is chaotic, we use the averaging argument of Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm together with a logarithmic improvement of the Efron-Stein inequality due to Benaïm and Rossignol.
papers.lean_note: All results are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, developed with AI agents, in a public repository that also covers the companion lattice paper.

papers.title: Persistence of Unitary Almost Mathieu Operator Gaps Ten Dry Martinis, Five on the Rim
papers.abstract: We determine exactly which gap labels are realized by open spectral gaps for the unitary almost Mathieu operator at every irrational frequency and all coupling constants ($0<λ_1,λ_2\leq1$). When both couplings are strictly less than one, every permitted gap label is realized by an open gap, including in the critical case ($λ_1=λ_2$). When at least one coupling equals one, both lifts of every odd winding label are realized by open gaps, whereas all even winding labels are collapsed. The proof combines quantitative almost reducibility and Aubry duality with a monotonicity principle for gap heights.
papers.lean_note: The main gap-labeling theorem is stated in Lean using Mathlib definitions and formally verified, with a Lean statement and verification index in Appendix C.

papers.title: Counting Square Tilings with a Fixed Set of Polyominoes Is #EXP-Complete
papers.abstract: An important question in counting complexity is whether exact counting can remain hard under restrictions that make feasibility easy. Tilings of squares by a fixed family of polyominoes provide a stringent test of this question, since tileability is polynomial-time decidable and the only varying input is a binary-encoded side length. We prove that there exists a fixed finite family of connected polyominoes for which counting translation-only square tilings is #EXP-complete under polynomial-time metric reductions, while the counting function belongs to #E. The resulting separation reveals that solution multiplicities can retain computational information that feasibility alone cannot capture. The proof develops a two-stage numerical isolation technique that combines a boundary-amplified Wang system with a rigid geometric compiler to recover accepting-computation counts while controlling all noncanonical tilings.
papers.lean_note: The authors provide a companion Lean 4 formalization of the #EXP-completeness result for counting fixed-polyomino square tilings.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
papers.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.
papers.lean_note: A certificate compiler generates Lean 4 proofs of stability, safety, docking, capture and SO(3) decrease properties for the champion controllers, checked by the Lean kernel.

papers.title: On sign patterns of Fourier coefficients of theta quotients
papers.abstract: Motivated by conjectures of Schlosser and Zhou on sign patterns of Fourier coefficients of infinite products, we study two families of theta quotients and their positive integral powers. We determine asymptotic formulas for their Fourier coefficients and use them to obtain explicit eventual periodic sign patterns. Our results provide new instances of the sign phenomena observed by Schlosser and Zhou and illustrate how dominant cusps determine the resulting sign patterns. These results were formalized and verified in Lean by AxiomProver.
papers.lean_note: The paper's asymptotic and sign-pattern results were formalized and verified in Lean by AxiomProver, with files in a public GitHub repository.

papers.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
papers.abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches 78.74 Recall@16 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer) and widens the margin to 7xrecall on competition-style queries. Downstream, its selected premises raise Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@4 on miniF2F-test from 49.90 to 54.03 and improve all four general-purpose LLMs on the informal IMO-ProofBench (up to +11.4% relative). Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.
papers.lean_note: Extracts typed Mathlib4 and Lean Blueprint dependency graphs to train a premise selector that supplies premises to Lean 4 LLM provers.

papers.title: Faster-than-power-law decay of order parameter correlations in the two-dimensional RP$^2$ model: a rigorous result by vibe-proving
papers.abstract: We consider the RP$^2$ model on the two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. It is obtained by replacing the spin in the standard classical Heisenberg model with a director, which does not distinguish two opposite directions. Unlike the standard classical Heisenberg model or the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, the RP$^2$ (and its cousin RP$^3$) model allows point vortex defects classified by $π_1(RP^2)= Z_2$ in two dimensions. It is tempting to expect the $Z_2$ vortices to induce a phase transition analogous to the well-established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(2) model (XY model) in two dimensions. Indeed, the possibilities of a critical phase or a critical point with power-law correlations of the order parameter in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models have been discussed in the literature. However, the challenging nature of the problem has prevented a definitive conclusion on the phase diagram so far. In this paper, we report a rigorous mathematical proof by Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 6 Astra) that the absolute value of the two-point correlation function of order parameters at distance $r$ in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models on the two-dimensional square lattice is bounded above by $C_β\exp{(-c_β[\log(2+r)]^2)}$ for any finite inverse temperature $β\ge0$, with positive constants $C_β$ and $c_β$ depending only on $β$. Namely, the correlation function decays faster than any power of $r$. The proof is formalized and verified in Lean; the formalization is publicly available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23548847 . A heuristic argument based on a one-parameter effective theory ansatz at large distances combined with the rigorous correlation bound suggests (but does not prove) that the $Z_2$ vortices are always unbound at any nonzero temperature.
papers.lean_note: AI-generated proof of super-polynomial correlation decay in RP^2 and RP^3 lattice models, fully formalized in Lean 4 against pinned Mathlib and archived on Zenodo.

papers.title: Iris on Indirection Theory: Lightweight Higher-order Ghost State
papers.abstract: Today, semantic models of languages with concurrency and higher-order state are constructed using step-indexed predicates over resources and higher-order ghost state. There are two main lines of work for constructing such models. On the one hand, Iris provides these in full generality, at the cost of a large body of mechanised domain theory that is difficult to learn and port to new proof assistants. On the other hand, Indirection Theory is much simpler through the use of ordinary dependent types, but its foundation in separation algebra limits the expressiveness of its resource model compared to Iris-style higher-order ghost state. We resolve this conundrum by showing that Indirection Theory can be as expressive as Iris. To that end, we give a lightweight mechanisation of Indirection Theory in Lean, generalised so knots contain resources from an Iris-style resource algebra functor. We then reconstruct the Iris base logic on top of it. The advantage of this approach is in the elementary metatheory: a user can follow the whole construction without domain theory. We conduct two case studies to show that the base logic is expressive and faithful to Iris: a biorthogonal logical relation for higher-order state, and an Iris-style program logic with invariants and user-definable ghost state, complete enough to verify concurrent and higher-order programs.
papers.lean_note: Mechanises Indirection Theory in Lean with Iris-style resource algebra functors, reconstructs the Iris base logic, and builds logical relations and a program logic.

papers.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
papers.abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.
papers.lean_note: Lean formally checks the algebraic certificate behind the main prime-power EAQECC family theorem; Lean sources with pinned dependencies and kernel/Comparator records are released.

papers.title: An explicit bound on the extremal function for complete graph minors
papers.abstract: Kostochka and Thomason independently proved that every graph with density at least $β\,t\sqrt{\log t}$ has a $K_t$ minor, for some constant $β$. Thomason later proved that the least such density is $(0.319\ldots+o(1))\,t\sqrt{\log t}$. However, the $o(1)$ term in this formula is not explicit, so the formula gives no bound for any specific value of $t$. The goal of this paper is a bound of the form $β\,t\sqrt{\log t}$ that holds for every $t$, with $β$ small. We prove that, for every integer $t\geqslant2$, every graph with density at least $4.5\,t\sqrt{\log t}$ has a $K_t$ minor.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem, including all numerical computations, is formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, and the Lean files are provided as arXiv ancillary files.

papers.title: Simple Cuts, Simple Landscape: Dimension-Free Rank Bounds for Burer-Monteiro Factorizations via Rank-Width
papers.abstract: In this work, we study Burer-Monteiro factorizations of semidefinite programs with unit diagonal constraints. For a real symmetric cost matrix whose rank-width over $\mathbb{R}$ is at most $k$, we prove that every non-flat second-order stationary point of the factorized problem is globally optimal whenever the factorization rank is at least $2k$, independently of the matrix size.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem and the key energy lower bounds were formally verified in Lean 4, with Lean source files provided as ancillary material.

papers.title: The Cranston--Li--Su--Wang--Xu (2026) conjecture is true
papers.abstract: Let $A$ be a finite abelian group. A nowhere-zero $A$-flow of a graph can be changed along a cycle: going around the cycle, add a fixed non-zero element of $A$ to the value of every edge that points forward and subtract it from the value of every edge that points backward. The Cranston--Li--Su--Wang--Xu (2026) conjecture on the reconfiguration of nowhere-zero flows states that if $A$ has at least four elements, then in every graph in which all degrees are even, any two nowhere-zero $A$-flows are joined by a chain of such changes through nowhere-zero $A$-flows. It also states that, for every integer $k\ge 4$, the same holds for integer flows whose values are between $1$ and $k-1$ in absolute value, where each change adds a non-zero integer. We prove this conjecture. The proof is by induction on the number of edges. If a flow enters a vertex along one edge and leaves it along another edge with the same value, the two edges can be replaced by a single edge; this gives a smaller graph. The main step is to change every flow into a flow with such a pair of edges. For $A$-flows we do this when all degrees are at most $4$; repeatedly replacing a vertex of degree at least $6$ by a triangle, following Cranston et al., reduces the general case to this one. For integer flows, we show that, in a graph in which all degrees are even, any two nowhere-zero flows with values in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_k$, $k\ge 4$, are joined by changes that add only $1$, $-1$, $2$ or $-2$, and that such changes lift to integer flows. All theorems of this paper are also proved in the Lean 4 proof assistant.
papers.lean_note: All theorems on reconfiguration of nowhere-zero flows in even graphs are formalized in Lean 4, with a public repository of the proofs.

papers.title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions
papers.abstract: Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.
papers.lean_note: Main theorems, lemmas, and the correctness of the decoupling algorithm are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, and the decoupling algorithm is also implemented as a Lean program.

papers.title: Classical communication over quantum channels: does entanglement help in nature?
papers.abstract: Can entangling codewords across independent uses of a quantum channel improve the rate of classical communication? An old conjecture states that there is no such entanglement advantage for all channels. Although Hastings's result and follow-up works disproved this conjecture, it turns out that enormous dimension is required to construct a channel where entanglement enhances classical communication. This indicates that there might be no entanglement advantage for many physical channels, or for all low dimensional channels. Motivated by recent progress on (generalized) amplitude damping channels, we propose a general Schur-weighted block entropy inequality, and show that there is no entanglement advantage for all phase-covariant channels including multi-level amplitude damping channels, generalized dephasing channels, and damping-dephasing channels. As a by-product, we also recover the recently established result that there is no entanglement advantage for all qubit channels.
papers.lean_note: All results, including the Schur-weighted block entropy inequality and strong additivity theorems, are fully verified in Lean with an accompanying repository.

papers.title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science
papers.abstract: Automated computational science could accelerate discovery by selecting, adapting and developing numerical methods. This prospect requires mathematical knowledge that AI systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. Here we present FARMS, a faithful and efficient foundation that transforms computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge. FARMS connects formal statements to source context, algorithmic meaning and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations and semantic review. Across 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline, with mean estimated costs of US \$0.85-2.29 per target across sources. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises connect selected statements to computational skills, illustrated by a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression. FARMS therefore supports an affordable, reusable knowledge foundation for trustworthy automated computational science.
papers.lean_note: An LLM-agent pipeline formalizes numerical linear algebra and PDE textbook statements as Lean declarations, then chains them via Lean-checked implications using Mathlib.

papers.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
papers.abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures.
