papers.lean_note: Mechanizes QPPM semantics, Hoare logic, verified lowering and optimization, and approximation bounds in Lean with Mathlib, and uses Lean kernel-checked certificates on benchmarks.

papers.title: Finite Mass Response to Vanishing Perturbations at Cauchy Horizons
papers.abstract: Smooth transverse perturbations with vanishing $L^p$ norm, for fixed finite $p\ge4$, can leave a finite positive mass increment at a Cauchy horizon. We prove this at a critical surface-gravity relation in the spherical Einstein--Maxwell--scalar system with positive cosmological constant. Each solution has bounded mass and local finite-energy weak extensions. The response escapes every fixed time window. An analytic law determines its delay and duration, and resolves enhancement or cancellation for overlapping packets.
papers.lean_note: The paper's mathematical results and proofs on mass response at Cauchy horizons are formalized in Lean 4, with a public repository and verification instructions.

papers.title: Agentic Verified Optimization of Real-World Software
papers.abstract: Program optimization aims to improve performance while preserving behavior. Coding agents can already make programs faster by changing algorithms, data structures, and execution strategies. However, existing equivalence checks mostly rely on tests, which agents have been shown to exploit, passing the tests without preserving the intended behavior. We propose agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation together with a machine-checked proof of equivalence to the existing one. Because the existing implementation serves as the specification, the task avoids the specification-writing bottleneck of verified code generation, and recent advances in theorem proving make the proofs attainable. We formulate the task at the function and repository levels in Lean 4, where programs can be both executed and reasoned about. Few real-world applications are written in Lean, so we develop Aqueduct, an agentic framework that migrates C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean, validates each port by differential testing against its original. On the 189 reference implementations in Verina, agents produce faster proved rewrites for 156, including algorithmic changes such as replacing exponential recursion with dynamic programming. On 17 migrated applications, their 92 proved rewrites speed up 47 of 51 application scenarios. These application-level gains are smaller than the function-level ones, making the choice of functions to optimize an important problem. Current agents can thus already carry out verified optimization on both standalone functions and applications migrated from real programs. We discuss the remaining challenges and the steps toward verified optimization in production.
papers.lean_note: Agents write faster Lean 4 implementations with kernel-checked equivalence proofs against reference functions, including C/C++/Go/Rust programs migrated into Lean.

papers.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $τ^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
papers.lean_note: Two integrity theorems (Action Integrity and Reasoning Integrity as noninterference) for the single-user memory interface are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.
papers.lean_note: Lean 4 with Mathlib machine-checks the algebraic skeleton of the paper's theory, including the width-center formula, the crossover identity and the limit claims.

papers.title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
papers.abstract: We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean~4.
papers.lean_note: All theorems, lemmas, propositions and corollaries are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, developed with LLM assistance and checked by an axiom audit.

papers.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $ω\le9/4$
papers.abstract: We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $ω\le9/4$. In a recent breakthrough, OpenAI~\cite{original} established this bound in the model of exact scalar arithmetic over the complex numbers, using non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $γ>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+γ})$ integer arithmetic operations. As an independent contribution, we develop a framework of \emph{polynomial packings}---methods for reducing many polynomial multiplications to fewer ones using linear operations. We isolate and generalize a construction of OpenAI~\cite{original} to obtain a simple packing, and show how packings can be composed to amplify their ``compression rate", which finally yields Strassen-like identities.
papers.lean_note: Aristotle generated an approximately 3,600-line Lean 4 formalization of the matrix-multiplication identities and the operation bound, using Mathlib's matrix definitions.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.
papers.lean_note: Provides a Lean 4 mechanization of the PC2 framework and its compliance theorems; agents submit Lean proofs checked by the Lean kernel before tool calls run.

papers.title: Thin-Layer Dichotomy in Three-Phase Mullins-Sekerka Flow: Gap Dynamics and Composite Interfaces
papers.abstract: We study the thin-layer limit of the Mullins-Sekerka flow in concentric circular geometries at fixed wave number $k$, contrasting a two-phase annulus with a genuine three-phase layer. A dichotomy emerges: for $k\ge2$ the rates blow up like the inverse thickness when the same phase lies on both sides of the layer, whereas between two different phases the matrix governing the linearized Fourier mode extends analytically to zero thickness. Both cases share the singular Dirichlet-to-Neumann factor of the thin annulus and differ only in whether the Gibbs-Thomson law forces an order-one potential difference across it. In the three-phase case the pure thickness-modulation rate stays below the logarithmic growth rate of the mean thickness, for every $k\ge1$ and all positive tensions, and, after projection onto the mean displacement and the outer interface, the collapsed pair moves as one interface carrying the sum of the two tensions. All statements concern the instantaneous fixed-mode linearization. The singularity is a property of the phase coupling, not of the thin geometry.
papers.lean_note: Selected results on the fixed-mode linearized Mullins–Sekerka system were formalized in Lean 4, with AI assistants helping develop the formalization.

papers.title: A Complete Dichotomy for $L_\infty$ Permutation Removal
papers.abstract: We study the removal problem for permutation patterns under the normalized $L_\infty$ earth mover's distance. We prove a complete dichotomy. Let \[ \mathcal E =\{(12),(21),(132),(213),(231),(312)\}. \] If $σ\in\mathcal E$, then every permutation of length $n$ that is $\varepsilon$-far from being $σ$-free contains at least $\varepsilon(n-1)$ copies of $σ$; for $0<\varepsilon\le 1/16$, this is sharp up to a constant factor for all sufficiently large $n$. If $σ\in S_k\setminus\mathcal E$, then for every sufficiently large $n$ there is a permutation of length $n$ that is $1/(8k)$-far from being $σ$-free and contains exactly one copy of $σ$. Thus the usual positive-density removal conclusion fails for every nontrivial permutation pattern, but the sparse behavior is completely characterized: the minimum number of copies is linear for exactly six patterns and is one for all others. Consequently, no canonical one-sided tester that rejects only after finding a forbidden copy can have query complexity independent of the permutation length.
papers.lean_note: All theorems, lemmas and constructions are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with the Lean code produced by an AI (Claude) formalize-paper workflow; repository provided.

papers.title: Non-expansive maps between unit balls that send the sphere onto the sphere are linear isometries
papers.abstract: Let $X$, $Y$ be real Banach spaces with closed unit balls $B_X$, $B_Y$ and unit spheres $S_X$, $S_Y$. We prove that every non-expansive map $F\colon B_X\to B_Y$ with $F(S_X)\subseteq S_Y\subseteq F(B_X)$ is the restriction of a surjective linear isometry $X\to Y$. Consequently, a non-expansive bijection of $B_X$ onto itself that fails to be an isometry must map some point of $S_X$ into the open unit ball, so the plasticity of $B_X$ reduces to showing that non-expansive bijections preserve norm 1. The proof shows that $F$ is Fréchet differentiable at $0$ with a surjective linear isometry $T$ as its derivative, and then proves $T^{-1}F=\mathrm{id}$ using a quantitative rigidity lemma for non-expansive self-maps $H$ of $B_X$ satisfying $\|a+H(a)\|=2$ for $a\in S_X$; the latter relies on the Baillon-Bruck rate of asymptotic regularity for Krasnosel'skii-Mann iterations. As a corollary, the identity is extremal in the set of non-expansive self-maps of $B_X$ for every Banach space $X$, which together with a result of Bargetz, Dymond and Pirk shows that all surjective isometries of $B_X$ are extremal, answering a question of theirs, including the case of $L^1[0,1]$.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem and the key rigidity lemma were formally proved in Lean, with statements and proofs hosted on the Prove2Me platform.

papers.title: Irrationality exponents of logarithmic numbers: Values, quotients, and graded approximation
papers.abstract: We establish degree-dependent irrationality-exponent bounds for logarithms at algebraic arguments and sharper bounds when conjugate logarithms match. A two-torus construction gives an upper bound of three for ratios of logarithms of multiplicatively independent positive rational numbers. We also treat normalized quadratic logarithms and circular logarithms. The rational-logarithm and rational-power exponent-two cases were treated earlier by Liu, Jiang and Zhang; we retain them within the broader framework and its Lean verification. Starting from the interpolation and determinant method in OpenAI's September 24, 2026 preprint on the irrationality exponent of $π$, we track the arithmetic cost of algebraic embeddings and the effects of matching conjugate logarithms. A second, graded Pade construction gives near-optimal measures for powers and bounded-degree polynomial values at sufficiently small logarithmic arguments, with estimates uniform in both coefficient height and rational denominator. We state the branch, independence, parameter-order, and approximation-field hypotheses explicitly. The Lean supplement has reviewed endpoint correspondences for all 62 numbered results: 53 direct checked endpoints or compositions, and nine applications with named classical theorem inputs. Native proofs of those inputs and separate formalizations of every unnumbered assertion are not supplied. Appendix A gives the exact declarations, hypotheses, and verification evidence.
papers.lean_note: Supplies a Lean supplement checking endpoints for all 62 numbered results: 53 directly checked endpoints or compositions, and nine relying on named classical theorem inputs.

papers.title: New Directions in Irrationality
papers.abstract: Since Apéry's proof of the irrationality of $ζ(3)$, decades of work have explored integrals, hypergeometric identities, and recurrences with exceptional arithmetic properties, to discover the strongest quantitative bounds on irrationality measures for zeta values and related constants. Yet, most findings have relied on specially tailored families of such constructions, making their systematic extension difficult. Here we show how these constructions can be connected and generalized into a common multidimensional structure based on conservative matrix fields (CMFs), enabling a systematic discovery of new irrationality proofs and quantitative bounds for irrationality exponents. CMFs are finite-dimensional cocycles of compatible rational matrix shifts, and are shown to capture all the classical constructions developed since Apéry as one-dimensional trajectories. The initial point encodes the mathematical constants; varying the trajectory within a suitable convergence region produces different approximation schemes for the same constants. We use this structure to improve the irrationality measures of famous constants, yielding for example $μ(ζ(2))<4.62675$ and $μ(ζ(3))<5.4197$, and proving that $1,ζ(3),ζ(4)$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, yielding $μ(Aζ(3)+Bζ(4))<66.3$ for every $(A,B)\in\mathbb{Q}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$. The same approach demonstrated over other CMFs provides irrationality proving trajectories for infinitely more mathematical constants. We further construct higher-rank CMFs with explicit initial states for $1,ζ(2),ζ(3),\ldots,ζ(d+1)$, and identify the arithmetic conditions needed to obtain further, higher-order independence results.
papers.lean_note: The irrationality-measure bounds for ζ(2), ζ(3) and Aζ(3)+Bζ(4) are formally verified in Lean 4, assuming the prime number theorem, with sources released.

papers.title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
papers.abstract: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We study finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of an $L$-smooth nonconvex function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values when, on the set where $f$ is below its initial value $f(0)$, the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix of trace at most $LE$. For an initial gap $Δ$, let $T=LΔ/\varepsilon^2$. We show that the Gaussian two-point method used in fine-tuning needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it accepts only the steps that decrease $f$, and we prove that every randomized method requires at least $Ω(ET)$ calls when $ET\le d$, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In that range, every deterministic method requires at least $\widetildeΩ(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls. A deterministic method pays about $d$ calls for each direction it discovers, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism therefore multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$, up to logarithmic factors. Once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods require $Ω(dT)$ calls, just as they do without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions that satisfy the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns projections of the gradient, charged by their rank.
papers.lean_note: Key deterministic lower bounds and a three-point upper bound are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib and checked by the kernel (Appendix J).

papers.title: An orthogonality inequality in $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ and the double-cap conjecture
papers.abstract: The orthogonal neighborhood of a set in real projective space is the union of the hyperplanes perpendicular to its points. We prove that caps minimize neighborhood measure among measurable sets of fixed measure in $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$, for $n \geq 3$, with rigidity up to null sets. This yields the double-cap conjecture: a measurable subset of $S^{n-1}$ containing no orthogonal pair has measure at most that of two opposite open caps of radius $π/4$. The argument combines compactness of the Funk transform, rotation comparisons, and projective variations. We also obtain qualitative stability and determine the measurable fractional chromatic number of the spherical orthogonality graph. AI played an assistive role in preparing this paper. The formalization and verification workflow for a separate Lean 4 proof of the main inequality and double-cap result, based on a different argument, were carried out almost entirely using AI-assisted tools.
papers.lean_note: The main neighborhood inequality and double-cap theorem, with rigidity, are machine-checked in Lean 4 (LeanShadow repository) via a different, largely AI-assisted proof.

papers.title: Record Types Everywhere
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel calculus that models first-class environments and function application paradigms using standard record types. By proposing new extensions to general record types, we achieve a design that is remarkably simple and principled. We formalise this design in a core calculus and prove several desirable properties, including type soundness, normalization, and a simulation of the simply typed lambda calculus. Additionally, we extend the design with mutable references. The calculus, its semantics, along with the extension, and all stated properties are fully mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant, alongside an interpreter formally verified to be equivalent to the operational semantics.
papers.lean_note: The record calculus, its reference extension, all metatheorems, and a verified interpreter equivalent to the operational semantics are mechanized in Lean 4.

papers.title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions
papers.abstract: Approximate leave-one-out (ALO) refers to methods that provide computationally efficient and statistically accurate approximations to leave-one-out risk estimation. These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited. In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. Assuming uniformly bounded block sizes, we prove that the expected average absolute discrepancy between the exact leave-one-out loss and its ALO approximation is $O(\log^{3/2}(en)/\sqrt{n})$. Our proof technique differs substantially from existing approaches and relies on obtaining sharp bounds on the number of active groups whose status changes between the full-data and leave-one-out estimators. In addition to yielding stronger guarantees under weaker assumptions than prior work, our analysis provides new insight into the stability of sparse estimators under perturbations of the training data.
papers.lean_note: The main theorem's proof, initially produced by an automated agentic system, comes with a Lean 4 verification provided as a linked artifact.

papers.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
papers.abstract: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.
papers.lean_note: Correctness of the 55-addition 3x3 matrix multiplication scheme is machine-checked in Lean 4, using Mathlib's Matrix API, over general non-commutative rings.

papers.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
papers.abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.
papers.lean_note: About 27,000 lines of Lean 4 with Mathlib verify both directions of the characterization and the thin-case DP; finite case checks use native_decide.

papers.title: The algebraic and geometric classification of $3$-Poisson algebras
papers.abstract: $3$-Poisson (ternary Nambu--Poisson) algebras are the algebras of observables of Nambu mechanics, the generalization of Hamiltonian mechanics in which the time evolution $\dot f=\{f,H_1,H_2\}$ is governed by two Hamiltonians and preserves the phase volume; their $3$-Lie part also gives the gauge algebra of the Bagger--Lambert--Gustavsson model of multiple M2-branes. We give the algebraic classification of complex $4$-dimensional $3$-Poisson algebras (seven algebras) and of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent $3$-Poisson algebras ($38$ algebras and one one-parameter family) with both multiplications non-zero. We also describe the algebraic counterpart of the Inönü--Wigner contractions of physics: the variety of complex $4$-dimensional $3$-Poisson algebras has dimension $16$ and seven irreducible components, one of which is the orbit closure of the simple $3$-Lie algebra of the M2-brane model, and the variety of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent $3$-Poisson algebras has dimension $20$ and five irreducible components.
papers.lean_note: The multiplication tables of both classification theorems were checked formally in Lean 4, with the Aristotle AI system assisting the formal verification.

papers.title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
papers.abstract: Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically. We show that, at any fixed positive tolerance, a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. We also study group-$k$ consistency, which uses consistency of groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge2$. Finally, our experiments on nearly 8,000 registration examples quantify the frequency of these limitations in practice and show how the derived bounds can be used to check whether a subset of matches can be aligned within a point tolerance.
papers.lean_note: All proofs about maximum clique, maximum consensus, and group-k consistency bounds were formally verified in Lean, with the formalization publicly released.

papers.title: Class polynomial obstructions to canonical congruences for the smallest parts function
papers.abstract: We resolve an open conjecture by proving that the only "canonical'' Ramanujan congruence primes for the Andrews' smallest parts function, $\operatorname{spt}(n)$, are $\ell= 5, 7, 13$. Building on work of Ahlgren and Kim, we show that any such congruence forces square-index coefficients of certain weakly holomorphic forms of weight $1/2$ to vanish modulo the congruence prime. A normalized Borcherds product converts this into the vanishing of the derivative of a quotient of two oriented CM polynomials on $X_0(6)$. A quaternionic volume estimate in an Eichler order of level $6$ prevents that vanishing when a suitable inert discriminant is small. Treviño's character estimate supplies such a discriminant for every prime at least $10^{11}$. The remaining range is covered by the previous calculations of Ahlgren and Kim. These results have been verified in Lean by AxiomProver.
papers.lean_note: The paper's proofs were formally verified in Lean by AxiomProver, with the formalization files posted in a public GitHub repository.

papers.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
papers.abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.
papers.lean_note: Introduces a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized REU open problems, with agent submissions checked by Comparator, the Lean kernel, and nanoda.

papers.title: Rényi Multi-entropy for Stabilizer States: A Finite Field Gauss Sum Problem
papers.abstract: Rényi multi-entropy probes multi-partite structure beyond bipartite spectra, but its behavior in general quantum states and the entanglement structure it captures remain poorly understood. We develop a finite field Gauss sum framework for calculating it in stabilizer states. Within this framework, the replica contraction reduces to a quadratic Gauss sum if and only if the state is locally unitarily equivalent to a stabilizer state. We obtain analytic expressions for the Rényi multi-entropy of all tree graph states and large families of loop graph states. In contrast to their flat bipartite Rényi spectra, stabilizer states generically have nonflat Rényi multi-entropy spectra.
papers.lean_note: Key assignment-sum formulas (tree graph formula, core-2/core-3, triangle and four-vertex loop cores) are machine-verified in Lean 4, with code in a public repository.

papers.title: Two hidden layer suffice: the caterpillar net
papers.abstract: Every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a finite signed sum of maxima of affine functions, making maximum representation a central problem in the study of the expressiveness of ReLU networks. A now-disproved conjecture predicted logarithmic depth for maxima. Inspired by the proof by Brunck et al. (2026) that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, we give the Caterpillar Net, a nonrecursive construction for the maximum of $N$ inputs with two hidden layers of widths $O(N^2)$ and $2^{O(N\log N)}$. The construction has a direct geometric interpretation.
papers.lean_note: Results on two-hidden-layer ReLU representations of the maximum were obtained via AI-assisted proof search in Lean and formalized in a public repository.

papers.title: Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture
papers.abstract: In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any $n \ge k-1\ge 2$, any collection of subsets of $[n]$ not containing a $k$-sunflower has size at most $c_k^n$ for some $c_k<2$. In the $k=3$ case, this follows from the work of Croot, Lev, and Pach and Ellenberg and Gijswijt on the cap-set problem, through a reduction due to Alon, Shpilka, and Umans. We prove the conjecture for every $k \ge 3$.
papers.lean_note: The proof of the Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture was machine-verified in Lean 4, with the formalization to be released in the Palomar repository.

papers.title: A Type System for Communication-Safe Hardware Design
papers.abstract: Hardware components communicate through clock-cycle-sensitive protocols. Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), however, provide limited support for expressing these protocols or for checking that independently developed components agree on them. When components disagree, the composed design can perform unsynchronized exchanges or stop making progress. We call these failures communication-safety violations. Communication safety is thus a global property, determined by interactions between components. This makes it difficult to check modularly. This paper presents Pact, a typed extension of Anvil for modular verification of communication safety in synchronous hardware. Pact types describe message-passing, control-flow, and clock-cycle behaviour. Each component is checked against its type. Compatible types guarantee that the components compose into a communication-safe system. Pact also supports incremental design. It can check a subsystem before the rest of the system exists. The check produces a summary type that captures the communication behaviour left for future compositions. To reduce annotation burden, Pact infers types by abstracting payload values while preserving communication, timing, control, and fairness. These inferred types are optimal for the checker: whenever some checker-accepted types can prove compatibility, the inferred types can prove it as well. Type inference and type checking are decidable, and compatibility is decided by a sound and complete algorithm. We implement Pact by extending the Anvil compiler and evaluate it along five dimensions: detecting communication errors in incremental design, expressiveness on ten clock-cycle-accurate translations of open-source hardware IPs, compatibility-checking time, generated hardware overhead, and annotation burden. Pact expresses realistic protocols and verifies all ten benchmarks in reasonable time.
papers.lean_note: The metatheory proofs of the Pact type system, including the constructor correspondence, are mechanized in Lean 4 and archived on Zenodo.

papers.title: The irrationality exponent of the lemniscate period: A determinant proof with a Lean 4 formalization
papers.abstract: Let $Ω=2\int_0^1(1-t^4)^{-1/2}dt$. We prove that, for every real $ν>2$, there is $Q\geq2$ such that $q^{-ν}<|Ω-p/q|$ for every integer $p$ and every integer $q\geq Q$. Consequently $Ω$ is irrational and its irrationality exponent is two. The proof combines elliptic separated-weight interpolation, arithmetic denominator estimates, and an analytic determinant bound on a square complex-multiplication grid. The determinant comparison uses the same selected source columns on both sides. We give the integral-to-lattice normalization, the exact local-coordinate and common-multiplier transport, and the parameter order that makes the two bounds incompatible. The accompanying Lean 4 development proves the endpoint without additional hypotheses. Numbered formal references link the mathematical argument to exact declarations in the complete source distribution; an appendix gives the pinned build environment and the dependency audit.
papers.lean_note: Full Lean 4/Mathlib formalization proving the lemniscate period's irrationality exponent is two; numbered references link the text to exact Lean declarations.

papers.title: Rózsa: Certified Equational Reasoning
papers.abstract: When does one equation imply another? Stage 2 of the SAIR Mathematics Distillation Challenge required teams to submit solvers to answer this question for sets equipped with a binary operation. For these sets, associativity, commutativity, or any other algebraic property was not assumed. Each answer required a proof or counterexample that could be verified by Lean. Programs also had to respect fixed resource limits. We present Rózsa, a Python solver that searches for both kinds of evidence. It begins with simple tests and considers more extensive searches when those fail. To find a proof, it applies a given equation and derives any further equations as needed, keeping a record of each step. To find a counterexample, it searches for operations on finite sets. It also tests one fixed infinite model. The given equation must hold for every assignment, while the target equation must fail for at least one. In either case, Rózsa turns the evidence into a Lean certificate. The submitted solver solved 199/200 problems (99.5%) in the official main evaluation getting the 6th overall position. Additional tests show that the solver can prove many implications linked by long chains of known results, but has limited success with infinite counterexamples. We explain the search methods, how they fit together, and what the unsolved cases reveal about their limits.
papers.lean_note: Python solver for magma law implications emits Lean certificates (proofs or countermodels) checked by the SAIR challenge's Lean judge.

papers.title: The Four-Qubit Hyperbolic Quadric Has Contextuality Degree 315
papers.abstract: The contextuality degree of a set of Pauli contexts is the least number of contexts that every noncontextual $\pm1$ assignment violates. For the four-qubit hyperbolic quadric $\mathcal{Q}^{+}(7,2)$, with $135$ points and $1575$ lines as contexts, Muller et al. conjectured from heuristic searches that the degree is $315$ and that the violated contexts of every optimal assignment form a dual polar space $DW(5,2)$. We prove both conjectures. The lower bound has a short proof by hand: every doily ($GQ(2,2)$) of the quadric contains ten Peres-Mermin grids covering each of its lines four times, so every assignment violates at least three of its fifteen lines, and averaging over the doilies gives $1575/5=315$. The equality case is local: an assignment is optimal exactly when it violates one ruling of one grid in every doily. Using this as a SAT encoding, we show that there are exactly $240$ optimal violated sets, one orbit of $\mathrm{O}^+(8,2)$, each isomorphic to $DW(5,2)$. The same argument gives the first lower bounds $\lceil L/5\rceil$ for all quadrics with $L$ lines in $N\ge4$ qubits. The degree theorem is kernel-checked in Lean 4, and the completeness of the enumeration is certified by a DRAT proof checked by the verified checker cake_lpr.
papers.lean_note: The contextuality degree 315 theorem for the real four-qubit hyperbolic quadric is formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using generated data files and kernel evaluations.

papers.title: Exact Compilation and Resource Laws for Hidden Integer Feedback
papers.abstract: Hidden rounding carries dependencies through integer memory. We study finite-memory feedback with predictable inputs that differ by one on at most $C$ releases and with every output public. A shared preparation constrains future branches until a sequence of common-input releases synchronizes the conditional registers. Preserving those constraints yields exact finite-law compilation, polynomial in support width for fixed memory and participation budgets, with constructive discrete-Gaussian transfer and calibration. A commitment hierarchy quantifies the loss from releasing dependencies early and becomes exact at depth $mC$ for memory $m$. Strict examples include three levels with one participation and a discrete-Gaussian calibration gap exceeding 0.23. Charging actual preparation time gives a privacy resource law with a square-root remainder and a leading coefficient computable in polynomial bit cost at fixed parameters. Lean refinements cover the first-order privacy analysis and binary value algorithm; separate lemmas check finite-memory algebra and paths. Certificates establish multi-memory calibration and resource effects; workload comparisons include a finite-memory prefix-error lower bound.
papers.lean_note: Verifies the discrete-Gaussian kernel, floor arithmetic, hidden-rounding mixture, transcript semantics, and first-order privacy analysis in Lean 4 with pinned Mathlib.

papers.title: Power-of-two cycles in projective cubic graphs of large edge-width
papers.abstract: Heckman and Krakovski proved that every 3-connected cubic planar graph contains a cycle of length 2^m for some 2 $\le$ m $\le$ 7. We extend this to 3-connected cubic graphs embedded in the real projective plane with face-width at least three and edge-width at least 48; the cycle may moreover be taken contractible. The argument passes to the spherical double cover, where the planar theorem provides the cycle inside a subgraph of diameter at most 47, and the condition on the edge-width guarantees that this subgraph projects injectively.
papers.lean_note: An extension lemma and a sumset inclusion for twelve profiles listed in an appendix were formalized in Lean 4; the main theorem was not formally verified.

papers.title: The e-positivity of $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k(e_μ)$
papers.abstract: We prove that the partition division operator $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k$ preserves e-positivity, resolving a conjecture of Alexandersson and Dai. For $μ\vdash kn$ and $ν\vdash n$, we express the coefficient of $e_ν$ in $\mathrm{rowDiv}_k(e_μ)$ as a normalized sum of positive rational weights over closed walks on a finite directed graph of $k$-restricted partitions. The proof combines the Pieri rule and a root of unity factorization for Macdonald polynomials. As a corollary, we recover the h-positivity of the symmetric functions $A_{n,k}$ of Amdeberhan, Shareshian, and Stanley.
papers.lean_note: The main e-positivity theorem and the closed-walk coefficient formula are formalized in Lean 4, with a public GitHub repository.

papers.title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
papers.abstract: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.
papers.lean_note: Finite gadget lemmas and pair-invariance contradiction forms of the impossibility theorem are machine-checked in Lean 4 via Boolean encodings; other lemmas remain paper proofs.

papers.title: Function Contracts for Bounded Model Checking of C Programs
papers.abstract: Bounded model checking unrolls a program into a single formula, so a function holding a loop costs the solver a fresh copy of that loop at every call site. Function contracts break that coupling. Verify the body once against its contract, then replace each call by a stub derived from it. CBMC supports this through dynamic frame condition checking, applied at industrial scale, but with no formal account of why the replacement is sound and no characterisation of what the frame check costs. We present the function-contract framework for ESBMC. The clause syntax, both phases, and the first assigns enforcement the tool has had are all introduced here. Its technical core is an observational frame rule: snapshot the locations the contract does not permit the function to write, then compare them at exit. The encoding emits a number of verification conditions set by how many globals the program has, not by how many writes the body performs, while dynamic frame condition checking grows with the write count. That is a property of the encoding rather than a timing, so it moves with neither the machine nor the solver. The rule itself is the classical one; what we add is its bounded form inside a BMC encoding, with the pipeline's algebraic skeleton machine-checked in Lean 4 and the limits of that model stated. We evaluate on synthetic sweeps, SV-COMP tasks, an ANSSI X.509 parser, the FreeRTOS heap_1 allocator, and the ML-KEM reference implementation whose CBMC contracts we reuse unchanged. At the coefficient count FIPS-203 mandates, neither tool finishes on the monolithic route inside ten minutes, and both finish on the modular one. The framework is merged into ESBMC master. Contracts are what is left when unrolling runs out of room.
papers.lean_note: Machine-checks the algebraic soundness skeleton of the Enforce/Replace contract pipeline and observational frame rule in Lean 4 over an abstract state-transformer model.

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof goals into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.
papers.lean_note: Builds an agentic LLM harness that develops Lean 4 proofs and verified code, coordinating parallel workers in a shared Lean workspace checked by the kernel.

papers.title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
papers.abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.
papers.lean_note: Adds compiler-error-guided tactic repair to a Lean 4 neural proof search, evaluated on LeanDojo and Lean Workbook benchmarks.

papers.title: Studying proof data with proof theory: the case of AI-generated mathematics
papers.abstract: I present a method for analyzing large collections of formally verified mathematical proofs (e.g. OpenAI's) grounded in some historical and philosophical musings on mathematics in the age of AI. Many of the quantities involved, such as the size of a proof term or the number of redundant steps, are already computed by work on improving automated provers, where they serve as targets. My aim is to turn them into measurements of proofs themselves: compared against a reference library and against each proof's own cut-free form, checked against theorems they must obey, and controlled for how the proofs were compiled. With these instruments, I measure how (much) machine-generated mathematics diverges from human mathematics, and find that AI-written formal proofs realize far less of the logical compression available to them than human mathematicians do (31% against 73% in mathlib, and 55% against 86% on proofs that call no automation). These figures are broadly in line with reports from those who build provers and proof-improvement tools that AI-written proofs are often longer than they need to be.
papers.lean_note: Compiles AI-written Lean corpora and human projects against a fixed Mathlib version and measures the proof terms Lean checks, comparing their compression against cut-free forms.

papers.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
papers.abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
papers.lean_note: All results on multi-head attention head complexity are formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with the formalization generated by an AI agent.

papers.title: The minimum number of vertices of a triangulation of $\mathbb{RP}^5$
papers.abstract: We give a computer-assisted proof that every finite simplicial triangulation of real projective five-space has at least twenty-four vertices. Together with the construction of Guyer, Steinerberger, and Yang, this determines the minimum. A cup-product argument produces an induced subcomplex on sixteen or seventeen vertices. Transfer to the spherical double cover then imposes a covering condition on its lifted faces. In the sixteen-vertex case, a direct capacity bound excludes twenty-two vertices. For twenty-three vertices, a cochain extension argument reduces every relevant completion to one of 115 critical signed complexes; integer weights and exact covering certificates exclude all of them. The argument requires no assumption that the triangulation is combinatorial.
papers.lean_note: Several intermediate statements of the computer-assisted lower-bound proof have Lean 4 proofs; the full theorem is not formalized end-to-end.

papers.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D
papers.abstract: Despite having an asymptotically optimal rate of convergence on convex quadratics, the acceleration of Polyak's heavy-ball method and a characterization of its dynamics within more general settings have remained long standing open problems. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. [arXiv:2502.19916], and iii) give a higher dimensional cycling instance which is not covered by root-of-unity cycling.
papers.lean_note: The main arguments on heavy-ball cycling and 1D non-acceleration are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with the formalization generated entirely by AI.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
papers.abstract: Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements. We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.
papers.lean_note: ACE normalizes and aligns Lean statement pairs, generates Lean proof obligations, and certifies equivalence or inequivalence only when Lean checks the proofs.

papers.title: 51 Additions per Recursive Step for Rank-23 $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication, Machine-Checked over Arbitrary Rings
papers.abstract: We present a rank-23 bilinear scheme for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication that uses 51 additions per recursive step in the alternative-basis (Karstadt-Schwartz) cost model, one below Nielsen's 52 (arXiv:2609.06588). The count 51 itself was first posted, on a different scheme, by Stapleton and Perminov (arXiv:2609.32388), found by heuristic sparse-basis search; the present work is independent and complementary: exactness and breadth rather than a single construction. The scheme is valid over every ring, so it recurses on block matrices, and its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4/Mathlib. The count is exactly optimal for the scheme's equivalence class: we introduce an exact free-basis minimization procedure whose negative answers are exhaustion proofs, and use it to show that 51 is the minimum for this class, that 52 is exactly optimal both for Nielsen's class and for the class of the current flat-model record, and to sweep the complete Heule-Kauers-Seidl database of rank-23 classes. The sweep is complete: exactly four classes attain 51, all in a single HKS invariant family. We machine-check Stapleton and Perminov's scheme as well, and prove in Lean that their 51 is optimal for its class. Separately, we document a systematic gap between $\mathbb{F}_2$ and signed optima: the $\mathbb{F}_2$-optimal chains of a class typically admit no sign assignment under most of the class's integer sign models, and certificate lifting fails where a direct signed search succeeds.
papers.lean_note: Lean 4/Mathlib kernel-checked proofs that the 51-addition rank-23 3x3 scheme computes AB over arbitrary rings, plus a class-optimality proof via decide.

papers.title: A direct proof of Infinity in NF-0
papers.abstract: We give a direct proof of Infinity in the no-empty version of New Foundations, denoted NF-0, by establishing that every model of the specified theory contains an object that is not finite in a precise, internally defined sense. The version considered has extensionality, at least two distinct objects, no empty objects, and inhabited stratified comprehension: a stratified extension is supplied whenever it has a member. Finiteness combines a two-sided internally represented well-order with the exclusion of internally represented nonterminating strict transitive relations on inhabited subsets. Assuming all objects finite, partial bijections yield comparison and finite extrema of positive Frege cardinals. Positive exponentiation, singleton type-raising, and the least orbit of the genuine two-cardinal lead to the equation n = T(n) + 1. We prove separately, and in detail, that adjoining one point reverses internally defined parity: the key ingredients are a graph-rewiring proof of invariance under adjoining two points and one instance of stratified induction derived from the all-finite assumption. Since type-raising preserves parity, the cardinal equation is impossible. We identify the corresponding Lean 4 declarations and make explicit the scope of the formal verification. No model-existence or consistency theorem for ordinary NF is claimed.
papers.lean_note: A companion Lean 4 project (Lean 4.24.0, Mathlib v4.24.0) encodes NF-0 as a structure and kernel-checks the Infinity theorem.

papers.title: A curved three-dimensional simplex Hilbert transform
papers.abstract: We prove Lebesgue space estimates for a curved three-dimensional simplex Hilbert transform associated with the moment curve $t \mapsto (t,t^2,t^3)$. The analysis relies on smoothing inequalities for curved multilinear averages and on estimates for a three-dimensional anisotropic variant of the twisted paraproduct. The result has been formally verified in Lean 4.
papers.lean_note: The main harmonic-analysis theorem was formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib by AI coding agents; the proof is published on GitHub.

papers.title: Universal scaling and measurability limits of thermal-conductivity measurement by a nanoscale point contact
papers.abstract: Thermal conductivity ($κ$) measurement of a thin film is critical for developing thermal management materials in heterogeneous systems. A nanoscale point contact method based on scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) offers a unique approach to probe $κ$ with nanoscale spatial resolution in sub-100 nm thick films. Extracting $κ$ of a thin film from this method requires separating film, substrate, and interface contributions that are comparable in magnitude. Multiple unknowns make this extraction a high dimensional problem. In this work, we used dimensional analysis to reduce the number of variables to provide physical insights into the realistic bounds of $κ$ measurement. We show that the total tip-sample thermal resistance $R_{ss}$, originally a function of six variables, reduces to four independent dimensionless groups. These groups are used to construct a mathematical relation that captures the dependence of $R_{ss}$ on the governing parameters. The resulting analysis shows that the point contact tip-film-substrate problem is governed by a single dimensionless invariant, $Ω= R_{ss}κ_{\mathrm{sub}}t$, and two control parameters: the confinement ratio $t/b$ and the thermal contrast $κ_{\mathrm{sub}}/κ_{\mathrm{film}}$. From the invariant, we derive an amplification factor, set only by the contact geometry and the interfaces, that converts the uncertainty of a measurement into an uncertainty in the extracted conductivity. This factor scales with the ratio of the parasitic interface resistance to the film's sheet thermal resistance and bounds the film conductivity that a given contact can resolve. We apply the framework to a 14$\pm$1 nm Al film grown on SiO$_2$ to locate the measurement within the established bound. The framework then lets us map its thermal resistance with sub-100 nm spatial resolution and recover the local thermal conductivity.
papers.lean_note: The dimensional analysis and algebraic derivations were formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, sorry-free. Bessel-integral results were excluded because Mathlib lacks Bessel functions.

papers.title: Optimal single-track Gray codes from Gray-ordered necklaces
papers.abstract: A single-track Gray code of length $n$ is a cyclic Gray code of $n$-bit words in which every column is a cyclic shift of the first. For prime $n$ the longest possible period is $2^n-2$. Whether it is attained for every prime has been open since Hiltgen, Paterson and Brandestini introduced these codes in 1996, and optimal codes were known for primes $n\le 19$. We show that a conjecture of Degni and Drisko (2007) on the reflected Gray code order of necklaces implies optimal single-track Gray codes for every prime. Their list of necklaces, conjecturally a Gray path for prime $n$, closes into a Hamilton cycle of the necklace graph after $(n-3)/2$ explicit Pósa rotations, and such a cycle lifts to an optimal code. This implication is formalized in Lean 4. Together with computation it gives optimal single-track Gray codes for every odd prime $n\le 47$: for $n\le 37$ explicit codes checked word by word by a program independent of the generator, and for $n=41$, $43$ and $47$ codes obtained from the implication after the Degni-Drisko property was verified at these lengths by two independently written programs.
papers.lean_note: Formalizes in Lean 4 with Mathlib that the Degni–Drisko property at a prime n yields an optimal single-track Gray code; n=3 and n=5 cases checked by computation.

papers.title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Mixed-State Quantum Geometry
papers.abstract: Mixed-state quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in quantum metrology, multiparameter estimation, and the characterization of quantum many-body systems. Yet, unlike its pure-state counterpart, accessing mixed-state geometry requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation for the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD), posing a major challenge for resource-efficient quantum computation. Here we address the challenge and develop a novel quantum algorithmic framework for efficiently accessing the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) and quantum geometric tensor (QGT) of mixed states. Our key insight is to uncover a previously unexplored connection between the positive semidefinite structure of density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, enabling an efficient integral-based construction of the SLD. A rigorous complexity analysis further establishes the resource efficiency of our algorithm, demonstrating logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancillary-qubit overhead at fixed conditioning. Building on this construction, we achieve near-Heisenberg precision scaling for diagonal QFI estimation without quantum phase estimation and construct unified block encodings of the full QFIM and QGT under a bounded spectral-gap assumption. A complementary regularized algorithm extends efficient diagonal estimation to exponentially small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition. Our results establish a resource-efficient route to coherent mixed-state quantum geometry, enabling its direct integration into quantum linear-algebra algorithms without classical reconstruction and opening new possibilities for quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.
papers.lean_note: Lean 4 is used to formally verify the bulk–edge deduction behind the asymptotic relation β_K/(4K)→1 for the Gauss–Laguerre LCU coefficient norm; code is available on request.

papers.title: Tight weighted paging with delay via mirror descent
papers.abstract: We give an O(log k)-competitive randomized algorithm for weighted paging with delay. This improves upon the O(log k log n)-competitive algorithm of Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi (STOC 2020, SICOMP 2022) by removing the dependence on the number n of pages. Without delay, the optimal competitive ratio of randomized algorithms is Theta(log k), and since the lower bound carries over, our bound is tight. Our algorithm is fractional and combines mirror descent, used by Bubeck et al. (STOC 2018) for weighted paging without delay, with preemptive service, introduced by Azar et al. (STOC 2017) for online service with delay: when a request is served, an increase in the mirror descent potential is offset by preemptive service to other pending requests, with a budget derived from the mirror descent path. To obtain a randomized algorithm, we use the online rounding of Bansal, Buchbinder, and Naor (FOCS 2007) from classical paging.
papers.lean_note: The main competitive-ratio theorem is formalized in Lean 4, assuming only the BBN07 online rounding, with a public repository; the Lean code was written by Claude Opus under author guidance.

papers.title: Random Tournaments Are Asymptotically Almost Surely Link-irregular
papers.abstract: Bastien and Khormali (2025) conjectured that a nontrivial link-irregular tournament with $n$ vertices exists if and only if $n \ge 6$. Their work establishes the conjecture for $n \le 100$. We present a probabilistic argument for the existence of link-irregular tournaments with $n$ vertices when $n \ge 9$ to resolve the conjecture. In fact, we show that a random tournament is asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.
papers.lean_note: Both main results, existence of link-irregular tournaments for n≥9 and the a.a.s. link-irregularity of random tournaments, are formalized in Lean 4 (GitHub).

papers.title: Surface corrections and vortex energetics in the Thomas--Fermi limit of a self-bound unitary Fermi superfluid
papers.abstract: We study a spin-balanced unitary Fermi superfluid bound by an attractive $1/r$ interaction within an extended Thomas--Fermi density functional. Its large-particle-number limit is the Lane--Emden polytrope of index $3/2$. We prove the leading gradient correction to the ground-state energy and strong convergence of the density amplitude. A rescaled surface problem predicts the next energy correction and the leading integrated density error. Matching a vortex core to the polytropic bulk gives the energetic threshold of a singly quantized central vortex, including the constant beyond the leading logarithm. Linearizing the same surface problem predicts a local energetic threshold for collective surface excitations that, in the natural TF frequency units, decreases more slowly with particle number than the central-vortex threshold. Radial stationary, spherical Bogoliubov--Poisson, and axisymmetric real-time calculations test the predicted energy corrections and vortex matching, and resolve finite-size surface-mode minima whose approach to the continuum surface coefficient is followed to $N\simeq4\times10^6$. For the reference gradient coefficient the vortex constant is $c_1=-0.535$, and the surface Landau scale is $1.417\,ω_K(\hbar_{\rm eff}^2/2R_{\rm TF})^{1/6}\propto N^{-1/9}$; sector energies at $N\simeq4.6\times10^5$, computed after the fit, agree with the extrapolated vortex threshold to $10^{-4}$. These results distinguish the accuracy of the Thomas--Fermi bulk from the gradient physics that controls the surface and vortex core, and separate vortex energetics from the open problem of nonlinear vortex entry.
papers.lean_note: Algebraic and functional-analytic steps of the main theorem, Bogoliubov reductions, unit conversions and power counting were checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: Proving LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Correct and Safe: Floating-Point Verification in Lean and VerCors
papers.abstract: Modern statistical model development begins with a high-level specification in an automatic differentiation framework such as PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow, which is then lowered to a target backend by a compiler or implemented manually by a research engineer. In this paper, we study whether frontier language models can correctly perform the latter task by generating GPU kernels from high-level benchmark specifications. We introduce a framework in which a language-model agent uses Velvet, a program verifier for imperative programs embedded in Lean, to prove semantic equivalence between a high-level specification and a generated CUDA kernel under an explicit set of assumptions. It also asks the LLM to prove thread safety and data race freedom of the generated kernel in VerCors, a deductive verifier for parallel code. Our main contribution to the formal verification of LLM- generated GPU kernels is showing that a combination of Lean automation and language-model-guided proof construction can verify a broad set of basic neural- network building blocks over floating-point values, allowing LLMs to implement semantically correct and safe kernels. In our framework, floating-point verifications never rely on compiled code and are always checked via the Lean kernel.
papers.lean_note: Uses Velvet, a Lean-embedded verifier, with SMT automation and LLM-guided proofs to prove Float32 semantic equivalence between PyTorch specifications and LLM-generated CUDA kernels.

papers.title: Erdős-Gyárfás Balanced Five-Colorings
papers.abstract: A coloring of the edges of a complete graph with $r$ colors is balanced if the edges among any $r+1$ vertices use all $r$ colors. Erdős and Gyárfás (1999) conjectured that for all $r\ge3$ the complete graph $K_{r^2+1}$ has no balanced $r$-coloring. They proved the conjecture for $r=3$ and $r=4$. We prove the conjecture for $r=5$, the first new case settled in over two decades. There is no balanced $5$-coloring of $K_{26}$, and since $K_{25}$ has one, $K_{25}$ is the largest complete graph admitting a balanced $5$-coloring. We design a reduce--dispatch--enumerate workflow, where every machine step produces an artifact that can be independently checked. First, we use a machine-checked (Lean 4) proof to reduce the conjecture to a single extremal statement about the color class with the fewest edges: no graph on $26$ vertices has between $55$ and $65$ edges while every $6$ of its vertices span between $1$ and $11$ edges. We then search on the sparse class instead of its dense complement, which makes enumeration up to isomorphism feasible. With classical stability theorems for $K_6$-free graphs, we dispatch the five near-extremal edge counts analytically. For the exhaustive enumeration on the remaining six edge counts, we design efficient encodings with SAT modulo symmetries and parallel cube-and-conquer. We also certify all eleven edge counts: each of the $12{,}296$ subproblems carries a clausal refutation checked by the independent verifier drat-trim, and all $273{,}503{,}938$ symmetry-breaking clauses are also validated against the vertex permutations that justify them.
papers.lean_note: A Lean 4 proof, using Mathlib's Turán theorem, formalizes the reduction of the r=5 Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture to an extremal lemma on one color class.

papers.title: A note on the rectangular Schoenberg-Whitney theorem for clamped B-splines
papers.abstract: Wang et al.(Computer-Aided Design 40 (2008) 999-1008) proposed a knot-subsequence characterization of full row rank for rectangular B-spline collocation matrices. We identify an incorrect inequality in their Appendix proof, which invalidates the argument as written, and make explicit the endpoint and multiplicity conventions on which the criterion depends. The defect lies in the proof, not in the underlying result, which is valid under suitably stated hypotheses; in the lofting construction of Wang et al. these hypotheses are implicitly satisfied, so the lofted curves are unaffected.
